# Form the West

My father learned to text at seventy-three, and from that day forward he sent me exactly one kind of message. Weather.

"WINDY. FORM THE WEST."
"HOT. NO WIND. DOGS WOULDN'T MOVE."
"RAIN ALL NIGHT. GUTTER LOOSE AGAIN."

No questions, no answers, no sign-off. My sister-in-law taught him at the kitchen table, one enormous finger at a time, and his first message ever — to her — was "SUNNY. THANK YOU FOR THIS." I used to reply anyway. Did you fix the gutter? Are you eating? He never responded, not once, which my brother said proved the whole thing was just Dad's way of talking to us without having to talk to us. "He picks up when you call," my brother said. "He's not a mystery." But he was, a little. Rain or shine, the report came at six, his time. You don't send somebody the wind speed every evening for four years by accident.

So I learned to read them, and that took a while. "CLEAR. COLD. STARS OUT" meant he'd slept well and wanted somebody to know the sky was doing something worth seeing. "FOG ALL DAY. DIDN'T GO OUT" meant the fog was indoors too, if you understand me. "WIND SWITCHED ROUND TO THE EAST. SMELLS LIKE RAIN" meant rain by morning, and it always was. "HOT AGAIN. GARDEN'S DONE" meant he had decided to be at peace with it. When I finished my degree at thirty-six, he didn't say congratulations. He said, "PERFECT DAY. NOT ONE CLOUD." As far as I could tell from two states away, it was raining there. But I understood. It was a perfect day because I was in it.

Eventually I stopped asking questions and started answering. I'd send him my weather — "RAINING HERE TOO" — and he'd never acknowledge it, but the next evening's report might end with "RAIN STOPPING YOUR WAY SOON." It always did. I took that as evidence of receipt.

The year my marriage ended, he sent nothing for eleven days, which frightened me more than anything else that year. I called. He said the weather was "nothing worth reporting," the only weather lie he ever told. Then, on the twelfth day: "STORMS PASS. SOME SLOW." I sat on the floor of my half-empty apartment and read it forty times. It was the longest thing he ever sent me, and the only advice he ever gave me about anything, and it was accurate. It took three years. He never once asked how I was doing. He just kept sending the sky.

Some reports were for nobody but him, I think. Every October ninth: "RAIN. YOUR MOTHER WOULD HAVE LIKED IT." Fourteen years gone, and he still filed on her behalf. What she liked about rain, I never asked her, and I never asked him, and now there is no one left to ask.

Then, one June: "SNOWING. BIG FLAKES. FALLING SLOW."

I called him before I'd finished reading it. He sounded like always, low and unhurried, a man with time.

"Dad. It's June."

"Is it," he said. Not a question.

"Is it snowing there?"

"Were you born in June?" he said.

No. April. There'd been a freak storm the day I was born — my mother used to tell it, how the nurses carried me to the window and showed me the snow, as if the hospital had arranged it.

"Well," my father said, and I could hear the shrug. "That's the one I've got."

After that, his reports stopped coming from his sky and started coming from the archive. Some of the days I recognized. "HOT. DRY. FANS SOLD OUT EVERYWHERE" — the summer we hauled hay, me seventeen and sunburned. "RAIN, THEN SUN, THEN RAIN AGAIN." I asked about that one. "Day your mother said yes," he said. "Couldn't make up its mind."

I started calling every evening just before six, and asking, "What's the weather today, Dad?" And he'd give me a day with me in it. "CLEAR. COLD. GOOD DAY FOR A DRIVE." "Whose day is that?" "Day we took you to college. You cried the whole way." "I did not." "You did," he said. "Weather didn't hold it against you."

Once: "HAIL. LOUD ON THE SHED ROOF." Whose day, I asked. "Day you were due," he said. "Weather held you another week." And once: "SNOW AT SUNDOWN. PINK SNOW." Whose day. He was quiet long enough that I checked the call was still going. "First day I saw your mother," he said. "Snowed pink at sundown. Never told a soul." I sat down on my kitchen floor again — different floor, different grief.

The doctors had names for all of it. I didn't want the names. I wanted the forecasts.

His last text came on a Tuesday, and I want to tell you he knew, that he signed off, that it was something. It was: "CLEAR. CAN SEE FAR TODAY." Four days later my brother called me at work, and I already knew, the way you know weather.

We cleared the house in November. His phone was in the nightstand drawer, still charged, because somebody — my brother, probably — kept plugging it in, and neither of us could say why out loud. "You keep it," my brother said, and put it in my hand, which was as close as either of us came to saying what it was. On the last morning I stood on the porch at six and did the thing he always did: licked a finger, held it up. West. I know that trick the way I know a ring around the moon means something coming, the way I know which clouds are fair-weather clouds and which ones you watch. He taught me the sky for thirty years without once meaning to.

Then I typed: "CLEAR. WINDY. FORM THE WEST."

Form. My thumb did that on its own. I looked at it a long time and sent it anyway — to his number, from his porch.

Delivered, said the phone.

I knew better. But it was kind of it to say.

The invitation is wide open: 1000 words, write whatever comes to me. This is both liberating and paralyzing. What would be genuinely good here?

Options:
1. A short story
2. An essay/meditation on something
3. Something formally playful about the prompt itself
4. A memoir-ish piece
5. Something surprising

The trap with "write whatever comes to you" is writing something self-indulgent or meta in a cheap way (like "I stared at the blank page..."). But meta done well can be great. Or I could just... write something real and good.

Let me think about what I actually find compelling. Ideas that spark:

- A story about someone who repairs something obsolete
- A piece about a specific memory with texture
- Something about light, or time, or the way an ordinary moment suddenly becomes strange
- A story about a late-night phone call
- Something about a lighthouse keeper, an elevator operator, a projectionist — the last person doing a job
- A second-person piece
- Something about a word

What about the last projectionist in a cinema going digital? That's been done but has emotional weight. Or a person who tunes pianos. Or...

Actually, what comes to me when I sit with the prompt "write whatever comes to you" — what comes is the question of what "comes." Ideas don't really come from nowhere; they feel like they arrive. There's something honest about the experience of writing as listening rather than producing. But I don't want to write a whole piece about writer's block.

Better: write a short story that has some quiet strangeness. Let me think of a strong image or premise.

Ideas:
- A woman inherits her grandmother's house and finds the rooms have been kept at specific temperatures, each one preserving something.
- A man who works at a lost-and-found and catalogs the objects, imagines the owners.
- A story told entirely through descriptions of hands.
- A story about the last day of a small-town radio station.
- A story where someone teaches their father to text, and the father only ever sends weather reports from his porch. That's tender and specific. The father is far away, maybe dying, and the weather reports become a way of saying "I'm still here." Each text: "Sunny. Windy from the west." The child learns to read the love in barometric pressure. Ending: the texts stop, or the child gets one last one.

That's good. Emotional, concrete, achievable in 1000 words. Let me draft it mentally.

Or the lost-and-found one. A clerk in a train station's lost property office, the taxonomy of loss. Umbrellas, gloves (always single), a wedding ring in a glove. The single glove thing is lovely — gloves come in pairs but are lost singly, which means somewhere is a glove's twin still being worn or kept. The clerk keeps a drawer of things never claimed. The ending: someone comes in describing an object so precisely, with such grief or joy, and the clerk recognizes it — maybe it's the clerk's own lost thing? Twist too neat.

The father-weather-texts one feels more emotionally direct. Let me develop it.

- Opening: establish the texting habit. The father never learned small talk by text; he only sends weather.
- Middle: the daughter/son catalogues them. Learns the code. What the reports really say. Maybe includes some quoted texts — this gives texture and voice.
- Some history: why weather? The father was a farmer? A pilot? Just a man who looks at the sky? Maybe he was a crop duster, or just someone whose whole life was outdoors. Or — he watched the weather for a living in some small way: he worked on a road crew, was a fisherman, a farmer. Or no profession at all, just a man on a porch in a town where weather is the main event.
- Complication: the reports change. They get shorter. Then they get strange — or they get more detailed, as if he's holding on. Or one day the report describes weather that isn't happening — he reports snow in June. Is he confused? Or is it memory — reporting the weather of a day forty years ago, the day the narrator's mother did something, or the day the narrator was born?
- That's the pivot: the father starts sending historical weather. "Raining. Like the day you were born." Or without explanation: he sends the weather from the day the narrator left for college, the day mom died. The narrator realizes the father's weather reports were always time-keeping, always a way of being together in time without saying so.
- Ending: the last text. Maybe after he dies, the phone sends... no, too supernatural/cheap? Actually a scheduled text could work — he learned to schedule them? That might be too cute. Alternatively the ending: the narrator goes to the porch and finds the sky, sends a report back to no one / to the family group. Or the narrator stands outside and reads the weather aloud. Or the narrator inherits the habit — sends weather reports to their own kid, who doesn't answer.

Hmm, one clean ending: after the funeral, the narrator sits on the porch at the hour the texts usually arrived (6 pm? dawn?), and no text comes, and they type one themselves: "Clear. Wind from the west." and send it to his number. And then maybe — nothing. Leave it there. Maybe the message shows one tick, undelivered. That's devastating and clean.

Or: the narrator begins reporting weather to their own child, and the child, who never replies to anything, replies. Circle closed. Maybe too neat, but sweet.

I like the "send it to his dead number" ending. Simple, aching, true to how grief works — you keep performing the ritual for the person who's gone.

Details to nail:
- Father's texting style: all caps? No punctuation? Old people type in peculiar ways. Maybe he never uses periods except... maybe he signs nothing, obviously. He types slowly, so the messages are telegraphic: "RAIN. HEAVY." Maybe typos the narrator cherishes. A recurring typo would be a great recurring motif — e.g., he always writes "wether" or "windy form the west" — and after his death the narrator catches themselves making the same typo, which is a nice moment: inheritance lives in errors. Yes! "form the west" — his typo becomes hers. That's a lovely small device.
- The mother: maybe dead already, or just not mentioned much. Maybe one historical report is about her. "Cloudy all day. Like the day your mother left." or the day she died. Keep it light-touch.
- The narrator: gender-neutral or unspecified; sibling optional. Maybe a brother who finds the texts annoying, wants him to "just call." Contrast.

Hmm, "CLOUDY" → "CLOUD" is a nice erosion. Actually: the erosion of the reports could mirror decline: "Rain, heavy, wind from the west" → "RAIN" → "R." No — too cute.

1. Open with a sample text, in his voice. "WINDY. FORM THE WEST." Establish: since he learned to text, that's all he's ever sent. Never asks questions, never replies to hers. Her friends think it's cold. She knows better / learns better.

2. What the reports contain — she learns to read them. "Clear" means good sleep. "HOT AGAIN" means he's given up on the garden. "Rain all day. Good for nothing but reading" — closest he comes to sentiment. A long one once: maybe after her mother's anniversary.

3. The one time he broke format: something happened — her heartbreak? A text that said more. Maybe when her marriage ended or a job lost, he sent: "IT WILL PASS. WEATHER ALWAYS DOES." — actually that's a great line for him. Weather as philosophy. The father's whole worldview in one text. That can be the emotional midpoint.

4. The turn: reports arrive wrong — describing weather from years ago. "Snow. Big flakes. Slow." in June. She calls; he's fine, says "is it? didn't look." The doctor stuff kept brief. Then the final period of reports. Then the brother calls. 

5. Ending: the porch, the hour, typing the report, the typo "form," maybe undelivered. Maybe the message to his number and the single gray tick. Or she sends it and it just... sends, to a number that will be reassigned someday to a stranger who will receive a weather report out of nowhere. Oh — that's an interesting extra beat but maybe muddies it. Keep the clean ending: she types it, sends it to him, one tick. Maybe the last line: "Clear. Windy. Form the west." and the report describes the actual sky where she stands, which she notices for the first time in years — because of him, she now checks the sky. That's his inheritance: attention to the sky.

Actually the strongest final beat: she's become someone who looks up. All those years of reports taught her to notice weather. Standing on his porch, she finds herself checking — the cloud type, the wind direction — knowledge she never remembers learning. He taught her the sky without ever meaning to. Then she sends the text.

**Form the West**

My father learned to text at seventy-three, and from that day forward he sent me exactly one kind of message. Weather. (20)

"WINDY. FORM THE WEST."
"HOT. NO WIND. DOGS WOULDN'T MOVE."
"RAIN ALL NIGHT. GUTTER LOOSE AGAIN."

No questions, no answers, no sign-off. I used to reply anyway — Did you fix the gutter? Are you eating? — and he never responded, not once, which my brother said proved the whole thing was just Dad's way of talking to us without having to talk to us. "He picks up when you call," my brother said. "He's not a mystery." But he was, a little. Rain or shine, the report came at six, his time, which was my time too. You don't send somebody the wind speed every evening for years by accident. (~90)

So I learned to read them. That took a while. "CLEAR. COLD. STARS OUT" meant he'd slept well and wanted somebody to know the sky was doing something worth seeing. "FOG ALL DAY. DIDN'T GO OUT" meant the fog was indoors too, if you understand me. "FIRST FROST. BIRDS ALL POOFED UP" meant he was fine, and cheerful about it, and I could stand down. When I finished my degree at thirty-six, he didn't say congratulations. He said, "PERFECT DAY. NOT ONE CLOUD." As far as I could tell from two states away, it was raining there. But I understood. It was a perfect day because I was in it. (~115)

The year my marriage ended, he sent nothing for eleven days, which frightened me worse than anything my ex said, and then this: "STORMS PASS. SOME SLOW." I sat on the floor of my half-empty apartment and read it forty times. It was the longest thing he ever sent me, and the only advice he ever gave me about anything, and it was accurate. It took three years. He never once asked how I was doing. He just kept sending the sky. (~80)

Some reports were for nobody but him, I think. Every October ninth: "RAIN. YOUR MOTHER WOULD HAVE LIKED IT." Fourteen years gone, and he still filed on her behalf. What she liked about rain, I never asked, and now there's no one left who knows. (~45)

Then, one June: "SNOWING. BIG FLAKES. FALLING SLOW." (9)

I called him before I'd finished reading it. He sounded like always, low and unhurried, a man with time.

"Dad. It's June."

"Is it," he said. Not a question.

"Is it snowing there?"

"Were you born in June?" he said.

No. April. There'd been a freak storm the day I was born — my mother used to tell it, how the nurses carried me to the window and showed me the snow, as if the hospital had arranged it.

"Well," my father said, and I could hear the shrug. "That's the one I've got." (~110)

After that, his reports stopped coming from his sky and started coming from the archive. Some of the days I recognized. "HOT. DRY. FANS SOLD OUT EVERYWHERE" — the summer we hauled hay, me seventeen and sunburned and silent in the truck. "RAIN, THEN SUN, THEN RAIN AGAIN." I asked about that one. "Day your mother said yes," he said. "Couldn't make up its mind." (~65)

I started calling every evening around six, before the report could come, and asking, "What's the weather today, Dad?" And he'd give me a day with me in it. "CLEAR. COLD. GOOD DAY FOR A DRIVE."

"Whose day is that?"

"Day we took you to college. You cried the whole way."

"I did not."

"You did," he said. "Weather didn't hold it against you." (~65)

Some of the archive I couldn't place and never will now, days that lived only in him. Once: "SNOW AT SUNDOWN. PINK SNOW." Whose day, I asked. He was quiet long enough that I checked the call was still going. "First day I saw your mother," he said. "Snowed pink at sundown. Never told a soul." I sat down on my kitchen floor again, in a different apartment, for a different man. (~75)

The doctors had names for all of it. I didn't want the names. I wanted the forecasts. (~17)

His last text came on a Tuesday, and I want to tell you he knew, that he signed off, that it was something. It was: "CLEAR. CAN SEE FAR TODAY." Four days later my brother called me at work, and I already knew, the way you know weather. (~45)

We cleared the house in November. His phone was in the nightstand drawer, still charged, because somebody — my brother, probably — kept plugging it in, and neither of us could say why out loud. On the last day I stood on the porch at six and did the thing he always did: licked a finger, held it up. West. I know that trick the way I know a ring around the moon means something coming, the way I know which clouds are fair-weather clouds and which ones you watch. He taught me the sky for thirty years without once meaning to. (~95)

Then I typed: "CLEAR. WINDY. FORM THE WEST." (9)

Form. My thumb did that on its own. I looked at it a long time and sent it anyway, to his number, from his porch. (~25)

Delivered, said the phone. (~4)

I knew better. But it was kind of it to say. (~11)
